1310.title: The Damdami Taksal
1310.hook: a school of recitation and exposition that traces itself to Baba Deep Singh
1310.howItsDone: Students of the Damdami Taksal live and study together, learning to recite Gurbani correctly and to give katha; the school traces its line of teachers to Baba Deep Singh at Damdama Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nihang speech, sava lakh, one rider counted as an army, and your line was one is enough. Today, a school with a mint in its name.

A coin from a careless mint looks almost right. The edge is a little soft, the face a little blurred, and after a while the shopkeepers start biting it to check. A coin from a careful mint is crisp; every line is where it should be, and nobody has to bite it. Year one stood in the Japji's workshop, where the Word is struck in a true mint. Today: a school with the word mint in its own name, one that sets out to strike readers of Gurbani as crisply as coins.
screen: `A CARELESS COIN GETS BITTEN.` → `A CAREFUL COIN IS CRISP.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR A MINT.`

segments.voice: Taksal means a mint, the place where coins are struck. The Japji uses it in its thirty-eighth step, on Ang 8, in paraphrase: in the true mint, the Word is struck. The Damdami Taksal is a school of Sikh learning that carries that word in its name. Damdami points to Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, where year three sat at the desk with Baba Deep Singh, copying the Granth one letter at a time. The Taksal traces its line of teachers back to him, and through him, in its own telling, to Guru Gobind Singh at Damdama: a chain of teacher to student, each handing on the same careful way of reading. The school strikes three things, mainly. Recitation: reading Gurbani aloud, steadily and correctly. Exposition, which Sikhs call katha: explaining what the lines mean. And the way of life around both, kept in the school itself, where students live and learn together. The Taksal keeps its own rehat on some points, and Sikhs hold a range of views about where it and the wider panth's code agree and differ. Today stays with what it's known for: care. Gurbani is meant to be heard and sung, not only read silently. A word slurred or misplaced can blur the meaning, the way a soft edge blurs a coin. So the students repeat, and repeat, and are corrected, until the line comes out crisp. Tomorrow sits in on that teaching itself.

1311.title: Learning pronunciation
1311.hook: careful teaching of how to read each word of Gurbani
1311.howItsDone: Sikhs learn santhiaa from a teacher, at home, in gurdwara classes or at schools like the Damdami Taksal: the teacher reads each word of Gurbani, the student repeats it, and corrections continue until the reading is right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Damdami Taksal, a mint for readers with a chain of teachers back to Baba Deep Singh. Your line was careful reading. Today, the lesson itself.

On a low stool, with a small prayer book open on her knee, a grandmother faces a small boy. She reads one word. He reads it back. She shakes her head, just slightly, and reads it again, a little slower, her finger under the letters. He tries again. This time she nods, and moves her finger one word along. A whole afternoon can go like that, and neither of them seems to mind. Yesterday's school is known for careful reading. Today we sit in on the lesson itself.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER, A BOOK, A BOY.` → `ONE WORD, READ BACK.` → `A NOD, AND ONE WORD ALONG.`

segments.voice: The word is santhiaa: teaching the correct reading of Gurbani, word by word, from teacher to student. It isn't a lecture; it's call and answer. The teacher reads, the student repeats, the teacher corrects, the student repeats again. Why so slow? Three reasons. First, the page. In the form installed in gurdwaras, the words of the Guru Granth Sahib run together, with no spaces between them. This is called larivar. So santhiaa teaches where each word begins and ends, because a break in the wrong place can turn one word into two and change the meaning. Second, the sound: how each word is spoken, vowel by vowel, so the line sounds the way the teacher received it. Third, the music. The hymns are set in ragas, to be sung, and a word placed right sits right in the tune. The Gurus keep this care in balance. In the Var in Raag Asa, Guru Nanak has a striking salok. In paraphrase: you may read and read, load up carts with books, fill whole caravans, fill pits and cellars, and read for a lifetime, with every breath. Only one thing counts in the account; all the rest is the chatter of ego. So santhiaa is not reading for its own sake. It's tuning the instrument. In the tradition's own picture, a correctly sounded line is a clearer door into the Name. The grandmother and the boy aren't polishing words; they're making sure the door opens all the way.

Your line: sound it right. Care with the sound is care with the meaning. Until tomorrow.

1312.title: The Akhand Kirtani Jatha
1312.hook: a movement known for all-night kirtan and strict discipline
1312.howItsDone: At Akhand Kirtani Jatha programs, the sangat sings Gurbani together, often through an entire night in a rainsabaee kirtan, repeating lines after the lead singers until dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, santhiaa, teacher reads and student repeats, and your line was sound it right. Today, a stream that sings all night.

It's past midnight in a hall with the lights turned low. Most of the city is asleep. On the floor, rows of people sit cross-legged, some swaying a little, some with eyes closed. A harmonium starts a line, and the whole room sings it back. Then again. Then a new verse. Nobody checks the time. Hours later, a gray light comes through the high windows, and the singing is still going. People call this a rainsabaee, a night that lasts the whole night. A group known for it is today's stream.
screen: `PAST MIDNIGHT, LIGHTS LOW.` → `THE ROOM SINGS IT BACK.` → `STILL SINGING AT FIRST LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Take the name apart. Akhand means unbroken. Kirtani means those who do kirtan, the singing of the Guru's hymns. Jatha means a band, a company that moves together. So: the company of unbroken singing. Tradition traces the group to Bhai Randhir Singh, a Sikh remembered for long hours of devotion and a strict life. Two things mark the Jatha. The first is kirtan itself. Its programs often run through the night, in a plain, congregational style. The sangat doesn't only listen; it sings, repeating lines together until the repetition becomes a kind of breathing. Members speak of that late, shared singing as a way the Name settles into a person. The second is discipline. The Jatha is known for keeping the rehat strictly, and some members keep observances beyond the common code, in diet and daily practice. Not every Sikh sees those extra observances the same way, and that question is left to the panth. What the Jatha leans on comes from the Granth. Guru Arjan, in Raag Maru on Ang 1075, says in paraphrase that in this dark age, singing the Lord's praise is the foremost thing. Kirtan isn't decoration on the side of worship; in that line, it stands at the front. And why the night? Gurbani speaks of the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, as a time for the Name. A night of kirtan walks straight into those hours instead of waking up for them. Few people can give a whole night to anything, but the shape still teaches: a song kept going long enough stops being a performance and becomes a place you live for a while.

1313.title: The Nanaksar tradition
1313.hook: a tradition of continuous kirtan and reading begun by Baba Nand Singh
1313.howItsDone: At Nanaksar centers, readers and kirtan singers take turns so that the Guru Granth Sahib's words are kept sounding continuously, and the Granth is served with detailed care as a living Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, the company of unbroken singing, and your line was kirtan till dawn. Today, praise handed on like a baton.

A relay race only works if the baton never touches the ground. One runner tires, and another is already moving alongside, hand out. Now set that race indoors, slow it down, and make the baton a voice. One reader finishes a stretch of the Guru Granth Sahib, and another is already seated, ready to go on without a gap. Down the hall, a small group sings, and when they rest, another group takes up the hymn. That is the picture at a Nanaksar gurdwara: the praise doesn't stop when one person does.
screen: `A BATON THAT NEVER TOUCHES THE GROUND.` → `ONE READER HANDS ON TO THE NEXT.` → `THE PRAISE DOESN'T STOP.`

segments.voice: The Nanaksar tradition grew around Baba Nand Singh, a holy man remembered for long stretches of solitary meditation and a deep, almost personal reverence for the Guru Granth Sahib. His followers carried on what he began, and Nanaksar centers keep it going today. Three things stand out. First, continuous praise: reading of the Granth and singing of kirtan are kept going in turns, so the Guru's word is always sounding somewhere in the house. Second, the Granth treated as a living Guru in very concrete ways. Nanaksar is known for care like that given to an honored person: food prepared and offered with great attention, the Granth's resting place kept with tenderness. The Granth is Guru for the whole panth; Nanaksar is known for making that honor detailed and constant. Third, simplicity of life for those who lead: tradition remembers the babas of Nanaksar as renunciants who asked little for themselves. Where does continuous praise come from? Open the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, on Ang 262. Its first stanza opens, in paraphrase: remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace. The repetition is the teaching. Simran, the word for remembering, isn't a single act; the hymn says it over and over, as if to show it should never quite stop. A Nanaksar center turns that line into the shape of a building. Sikhs hold different views about some Nanaksar customs and their place beside the common code. The aim itself is plain: a house where the praise doesn't fall silent.

1314.title: The Namdharis today
1314.hook: they keep white dress and simple rites, and differ from most Sikhs in following a living guru
1314.howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs wear white, tie the turban in a straight style, keep a vegetarian life with a wool mala for remembrance, marry in simple ceremonies without dowry, and follow a living satguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nanaksar tradition, readers and singers handing the Guru's word on in turns. Your line was continuous praise. Today, a wedding all in white.

A wedding in a courtyard, and everyone is in white. The men's turbans are white too, tied flat and straight across the forehead. There is no great feast of display, no long line of expensive gifts. A small sacred fire is lit, hymns are sung, and a couple is married simply. Some guests hold a mala, a string of beads, made of white wool. If you know Sikh weddings from photos of crimson and gold, this one may look like a different world. It belongs to the Namdharis, and today we meet them on their own terms.
screen: `A WEDDING ALL IN WHITE.` → `A SMALL FIRE, HYMNS, A SIMPLE RITE.` → `A WOOL MALA IN THE HAND.`

segments.voice: The Namdharis are a Sikh community whose name carries naam, the Name of God, at its center: those who hold to the Name. Year three told how the movement took shape, with Satguru Ram Singh, his call to simple living, and his stand against British rule that ended in exile. They're also called Kukas, and tradition links that name to the cries of devotion that rose in their gatherings. Today they keep three marks. White clothing, plain and often handspun, with the turban tied in their own straight style. Simple rites: weddings without dowry or display, around a small fire with hymns. And a strict life of vegetarian food and daily remembrance of the Name, with the wool mala close at hand. Then the difference, stated plainly. The wider panth holds that the line of human Gurus ended with Guru Gobind Singh, and that the Guru is now the Granth and the Khalsa together. Namdharis follow a living guru, a line of satgurus who lead the community today. That's a real difference, and Sikhs on both sides take it seriously. This path won't argue it out. It can listen to the Granth both sides revere. Guru Arjan, in Raag Kanra on Ang 1299, sings, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line doesn't erase disagreement. It sets a tone for living beside it: a difference named clearly, held honestly, and still met with respect.

1315.title: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris today
1315.hook: a reform movement distinct from the later Sant Nirankari Mission
1315.howItsDone: Sikhs distinguish Baba Dayal's Nirankari reform, remembered for calling Sikhs to the Formless One and for weddings around the Guru Granth Sahib, from the later and separate Sant Nirankari Mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Namdharis today: white dress, simple rites and a living guru. Your line was different, and respected. Today, two movements that share one name.

Two restaurants in one city share a name. One is a family place that has served the same dish for generations. The other opened later, with a different menu and a different owner. Locals never mix them up. Visitors do it all the time, and the family place keeps having to explain: that's not us. Sikh history has a pair like that. Two movements carry the word Nirankari. They are not the same, and today is about telling them apart, carefully and fairly.
screen: `TWO PLACES, ONE NAME.` → `LOCALS NEVER MIX THEM UP.` → `TWO NIRANKARI MOVEMENTS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Nirankar means the Formless One, a name for God that runs through Gurbani. In the Japji, from Ang 3, Guru Nanak closes several stanzas with a refrain, in paraphrase: you are forever safe and whole, O Formless One. To be a Nirankari is to belong to the Formless. The first movement: Baba Dayal was a Sikh reformer in the northwest of Punjab, in the city of Rawalpindi. Tradition remembers him calling Sikhs back to the Formless One and away from rites he saw creeping in: idols, priestly ceremonies, customs that pulled attention from the Guru's word. His movement is especially remembered for weddings. Nirankaris married by circling the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan, Guru Ram Das's wedding hymns, were sung: the anand karaj, the wedding rite Sikhs know today. Baba Dayal's Nirankaris continue as a community that honors the Guru Granth Sahib and remembers its founder. The second movement: the Sant Nirankari Mission is a later and separate organization, with its own living leaders and its own teachings. Sikh bodies have been in serious, painful disagreement with it. That story is heavy and deserves more than one sentence in a short lesson, so this path leaves it there. Why the distinction matters: when the two are confused, a reform remembered for the wedding around the Granth gets tangled up with a conflict it had no part in. Knowing the difference is a small act of fairness to both.

1316.title: Sikh Dharma in the West
1316.hook: Western converts since the 1970s, often in white turbans
1316.howItsDone: Members of Sikh Dharma, a community of Sikhs in the West, keep the rehat and the daily banis, sing kirtan in Gurmukhi, and worship and serve langar alongside Punjabi Sikh families; women as well as men often wear the turban.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two movements with one name, and your line was know the difference. Today, a stream that flows far from Punjab.

A gurdwara in New Mexico, or California, or Massachusetts. A woman in a white turban leads the kirtan, and her Gurmukhi is careful and clear. Her parents were not Sikhs. Neither were the parents of the man beside her on the tabla, who took a Sikh name as an adult. After the program, they serve langar alongside Punjabi families whose grandparents came from villages near Amritsar. Everyone sits in the same rows. It's the story of a stream that flows far from Punjab.
screen: `A WHITE TURBAN LEADS THE KIRTAN.` → `PARENTS WHO WERE NOT SIKHS.` → `THE SAME ROWS AT LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Sikh Dharma is the name used by a community of Sikhs in the West, among them people who came to the faith as adults. They first met it through a teacher of yoga and meditation from Punjab, known as Yogi Bhajan. His students took up the rehat: uncut hair, the turban, the daily banis, often an early morning practice before dawn. Women in this community commonly wear the turban too, and white clothing is a familiar sight. Two things need saying plainly. First, Sikhs have held differing views about this community: about the yoga it taught alongside Sikh practice, and about how its customs sit beside the Rehat Maryada. Second, its founder's legacy is now seriously contested. Former students have come forward with grave accusations against him, and the community has had to face them, with members responding in different ways. That is part of the story, and this path won't smooth it over. If this touches something in your own life, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help. And yet the newcomers stand on something older than any teacher. Guru Arjan, in Raag Dhanasari on Ang 671, sings, in paraphrase: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to everyone. A gurdwara with open doors and one row at langar was built for this: a stranger walks in, covers their head, sits down, and is fed. This week brought the Taksal's careful reading, santhiaa, the Jatha's kirtan till dawn, Nanaksar's continuous praise, the Namdharis, Baba Dayal's reform, and now newcomers who learned the Guru's word as a second language.
